Source guide
Summary
This text is a collection of prompts for Midjourney, an AI art generator. The prompts showcase a highly eclectic and imaginative style, blending diverse artistic movements (Art Deco, Art Nouveau, Surrealism), technological elements (steampunk, cyberpunk), and cultural references (Aztec, Mayan, Victorian). Many prompts feature detailed descriptions emphasizing realism, specific camera types, and unusual materials. The overall effect is a chaotic yet captivating exploration of highly stylized and fantastical imagery, interspersed with unrelated text snippets, including sections of a book, game rules, and personal reflections.

3 STANDARD ACTIONS [1 Backing chit unless otherwise specified]
- Propose a partial translation by playing a Gloss Card. If playing as your Character, play Gloss Card face-down on any Voynichese Word in the Manuscript common pool unless otherwise specified by the text printed on your Character Card. If playing as your Academic, play this card face up on any Voynichese Word in the Manuscript common pool unless otherwise specified by the text printed on your Academic card or any Voting Rules card in play.
- You may propose an Alternate Manuscript language using a Language Card in your hand. This triggers a Scholarly Consensus Vote among all players with face-up Academic cards, according to the Voting Rules in play. Turn Gloss cards in the Manuscript common pool face down except those matching your proposed Manuscript Language. Follow the instructions of the text printed on the card.
- Propose a Crazy Idea Manuscript Language. You may also propose a novel suggestion for the Manuscript Language without playing a Language Card by spending 2 Backing chits.
- Propose a partial transliteration: Play a Glyph card on any Voynichese card in the Manuscript common pool. Follow the instructions of the text printed on the card.
- Play a card that changes the Voting Rules. Follow the instructions in the text printed on the card.
- Flip your Character / Academic Card to change the play of your turn.
- Spend 2 Backing chits to flip your Character / Academic Card and change the play at any time during your turn.
- Contribute to the Manuscript lore by playing legend cards according to the rules on the card.
- Preserve one clue under a Preservation card in your Cache.
UPKEEP
4 - At the end of each turn, you must flip your Character / Academic card according to the instructions printed on it.
= = = = = = = = = =
Each author card counts as one Free Action when played in the final round.
= = = = = = = = = =
Each author card counts as one Free Action when played in the final round.
Voting:
If you call a vote and your translation achieves Consensus, then you may take an extra turn [or draw an extra card?]. If Consensus fails, you lose your next turn [or discard?].
= = = = = = = = = =
The Author Card: Each character has a corresponding Author Card. At the begining of a vote, the player who announces the vote draws a card. If you draw your author card, then you are the author of the manuscript, and you must look through the deck, removing all other Author cards from the deck. If any other card is drawn, you must look through the deck and choose seven(or whatever the number of characters is) cards of your choosing and place them face down in front of you. You may choose any cards in the deck, including any Author cards. These cards may not be used until the Final Round, in which they will replace your hand. You may not reveal the cards, nor whether or not you are the author (except by preserving evidence) until the end of the game. If you are the Author of the Manuscript, then begining with this vote, you MUST choose either to conceal your authorship by only voting against any Translation that indicates your authorship [e.g. votes that include any of Language(s) or Locality] or you must choose not to conceal your authorship by voting for any Translation that indicates your authorship. Once you have chosen whether or not to conceal your authorship, you may ONLY vote in accordance with this choice, you may not alternate. In either case, you may not reveal whether you are the author or not until the end of the game, except by preserving evidence.

Game objects, typically cards, have icons or other identifiers that identify them as belonging to specific categories. These tags may trigger special effects and/or have values and meaning that can vary, even within the scope of a single play. Tags are additional parameters on top of the base meaning of the game element, so tags represent a means of coupling the game element with more mechanisms and systems. Tags are also bookmarks that can reference a variable set of possible rules that are encoded elsewhere, so tags are also a means to modularize, or uncouple, game triggers and game effects.


= = = = = = = = = =

= = = = = = = = = =
In storytelling games, players are provided with conceptual, written, or pictorial stimuli which must be incorporated into a story of the players' creation. Once Upon a Time uses a selection of words while Rory's Story Cubes include ambiguous symbols. Some games like Snake Oil and Big Idea prompt players to pitch a product, which frequently takes the form of a brief story or vignette.

Other storytelling games include titles such as Tales of the Arabian Nights and Above and Below, game designs in which players don't create their own stories, but instead experience a story from the inside as one of the participants. Games along those lines might present players with a particular narrative situation, after which the player will make a choice that affects which end to the narrative is told — with the results of this narrative affecting the player's standing in the game.


= = = = = = = = = =
A game in which players are cooperating and competing with each other throughout the game, while trying to complete a common objective. To be classified as semi-cooperative, there must be two possible end states:

A) One or more (but unlikely to be all) players win
B) No players win

A game where players sometimes cooperate and sometimes compete but one always wins is not semi-cooperative. It is a Competitive game with a Negotiation mechanism.


= = = = = = = = = =
Secret unit deployment games are games that contain hidden information. Only the player controlling certain playing pieces has perfect information about the nature (or even the whereabouts) of those pieces. This mechanic is often used in wargames to simulate "fog of war".


= = = = = = = = = =
A game system that can be applied to a variety of different maps, starting resources and positions, and even different win and loss conditions. These variable conditions can be assembled into a broader narrative or campaign, or they can be entirely disconnected from one another.


= = = = = = = = = =
Some board games incorporate elements of role playing. It can be that players control a character that improves over time. It can also be a game that encourages or inspires Storytelling. This mechanic can be viewed as an extension of Variable Player Powers.


= = = = = = = = = =
Resources are generated from a random process and distributed to qualifying players.


= = = = = = = = = =
Players ask and answer questions in a manner constrained by rules.


= = = = = = = = = =
The Pieces themselves compose the Map.

This is distinct from Tile Placement in that the map elements remain “pieces” after placement, and accordingly continue to have agency in the game mechanics.


= = = = = = = = = =
Pieces are removed from a structure, and play is affected by things that fall (as in Ker Plunk), or a complete collapse of the structure (as in Jenga).


= = = = = = = = = =
Players possess one or more Action Tokens. Those who have an Action Token may take a turn, then they pass the token clockwise, allowing the next player to perform an action. Actions are performed in real time; - there is no pausing and structure within the turn.

Typically, to prevent stalling and to keep the game moving, in games with multiple Action Tokens, if both tokens are held by the same player, then they suffer a penalty.


= = = = = = = = = =
Players have a special ability that they can use one time per game.

These may be unique to them, like 'feats' in Warmachine, or common to all players, like the special power chits in Finca.

Often players will receive bonus Victory Points if they do not use their one-time abilities during the game.


= = = = = = = = = =
Actions, resources, or resolution are shared between neighbors.


= = = = = = = = = =
Multiple action options are presented to the players via a narrative format.

These can be presented in a book with numbered paragraphs as in Tales of the Arabian Nights or Above and Below, or via cards as in Dead of Winter: A Crossroads Game.


= = = = = = = = = =
Multiple actions are shown on a card, but only one can be used.


= = = = = = = = = =
Players Move Through a Deck of cards. Typically the goal is to reach the bottom (One Deck Dungeon), find and defeat a boss (Chainsaw Warrior), or simply know when to quit (Diamant).


= = = = = = = = = =
When a conflict is initiated, pieces are moved to a separate board for resolution.


= = = = = = = = = =
A set of cards in a specific relationship to one another that allows them to be played to a table or scored is a meld. When laying these cards down, the way the cards splay, or overlap one another, may sometimes reveal or conceal certain abilities or attributes.

Rummy games have players placing combinations of cards or tiles on the table to score. Innovation is a good example of the Splaying side, where players can spread cards out to show particular sets of icons to empower abilities.


= = = = = = = = = =
A set of cards in a specific relationship to one another that allows them to be played to a table or scored is a meld. When laying these cards down, the way the cards splay, or overlap one another, may sometimes reveal or conceal certain abilities or attributes.


= = = = = = = = = =
Players must make their next play by matching a feature on the previous play. This is frequently used in shedding games like UNO or Crazy Eights, where number or color/suit need to be matched.

In some implementations the next play needs to be in a number range based on the last. For example, in L.L.A.M.A. the play must be the same or one higher than the last. In Spit, it must be one higher or lower.

NOTE: Although this is similar to 'following suit' in a trick taking game, or 'ladder climbing' games, please use those mechanisms instead.


= = = = = = = = = =
Over the course of the game, the map shrinks.


= = = = = = = = = =
A multi-session game in which permanent and irreversible changes to the game state carry over to future plays. Components may be written on with permanent ink, torn apart, covered with a sticker, etc.


= = = = = = = = = =
Players contribute towards completing a task, but only the player who finally completes it gets a particular benefit or bonus reward (even if others share in the base level benefit).


= = = = = = = = = =
This is a meta-mechanic for Turn Order. Players may take an action that interrupts the normal turn flow.


= = = = = = = = = =
The number of Victory Points held by each player is private information.


= = = = = = = = = =
Movement occurs that is not visible to all players.

Scotland Yard is a classic game implementing this mechanism.

A key challenge for designers is determining how to make the movement rules simple enough that the players moving hidden units do not make mistakes, or that paths are traceable when the game concludes.


= = = = = = = = = =
Hand management games are games with cards in them that reward players for playing the cards in certain sequences or groups. The optimal sequence/grouping may vary, depending on board position, cards held and cards played by opponents. Managing your hand means gaining the most value out of available cards under given circumstances. Cards often have multiple uses in the game, further obfuscating an "optimal" sequence.

Hand management has no relationship to action/dexterity.


= = = = = = = = = =

= = = = = = = = = =
When the main game ends, a special mini-game is played to determine the victor.


= = = = = = = = = =
Different Dice are used to move depending on unit or game state.


= = = = = = = = = =
"Dice Rolling" is a game mechanism that can be used for many things, randomness being the most obvious.

In wargames, "Dice Rolling" is used in conjunction with a variety of tables, notably a "Combat Results Table" (either as a Ratio or a Differential) which produces a result by strengths of both sides and a die roll (1D6, 2D6, and 1D10 are most commonly used).


= = = = = = = = = =
Players are trying to determine the identity of hidden information based on clues.
= = = = = = = = = =
Dice are rolled, and those exceeding a target number generate a success. Certain rolls (typically the highest and/or lowest on the die) generate additional success or extreme failure.


= = = = = = = = = =
Players coordinate their actions to achieve a common win condition or conditions. Players all win or lose the game together.


= = = = = = = = = =
Games may limit players from communicating with one another openly. These restrictions can be absolute as they relate to certain specific pieces of information, or they may restrict certain types of communication, such as speaking.

Examples of this mechanism include Hanabi and Reverse Charades.


= = = = = = = = = =
Players have a hand of cards that allows them to activate and perform actions with a subset of their units.


= = = = = = = = = =
Closed Drafting (or 'Card Drafting') is a means of distributing cards or other game elements to players through an ordered, closed selection process - typically "select and pass".

A typical implementation involves each player being dealt the same number of cards. Players then select one (or more) card(s) to keep, and pass the rest to their left. This continues until all cards are selected or discarded. 7 Wonders implements this type of draft.

An alternative is that only one player is dealt cards, and they take one and pass it until all players have cards. This obviously is strongly biased towards the first player, and needs to be supported thematically and balance-wise. Citadels implements this type of draft.

This is distinct from Open Drafting, with involves selection from a public display.


= = = = = = = = = =
Pieces are stationary but are built out in chains. This can give a dynamic sense of motion to the game, even though the pieces do not move.

Early examples of this mechanism can be found in Expedition and Through the Desert.


= = = = = = = = = =
Each player simultaneously or sequentially plays one or more cards. These modify the base outcome of a conflict and allow various special abilities to apply.

This can function similarly to Area Majority / Influence, but with a discrete resolution or award of the conflict target, rather than by dynamic/shifting control of a fixed asset. It is also similar to Force Commitment, but that mechanic presupposes a more liquid resource where the quantity can be chosen.


= = = = = = = = = =
Each player has a set of Actions available to them, embodied in cards, tokens, or some other affordance. Once performed, they are spent and may not be performed again until retrieved. Action Retrieval typically is itself an Action, or may take an entire turn.


= = = = = = = = = =
The earliest example of a game listed on Boardgamegeek that uses AP's is Special Train (1948).
= = = = = = = = = =
A player receives a number of Action Points or Operation Points on their turn. They may spend them on a variety of Actions.

The earliest example of a game listed on Boardgamegeek that uses AP's is Special Train (1948).

= = = = = = = = = =
Economic games encourage players to manage a system of production, distribution, trade, and/or consumption of goods. The games usually simulate a market in some way. The term is often used interchangeably with resource management games.


= = = = = = = = = =
A strategy game is a game in which the players' decision-making skills have a high significance in determining the outcome. Strategy games often require decision tree analysis, or probabilistic estimation in the case of games with chance elements. Strategy games include abstract games, with artificial rules and little or no theme, and simulations (including wargames), with rules designed to emulate and reproduce a real or fictional scenario.

At some point a while back, I hit on the idea of "**opulent hyperbaric chambers**" and, liking the results, I just kept elaborating on that with all sorts of random modifiers like "Opulent hyperbaric wraparound-screen Victorian-Senegalese neohittite crustpunk fractal implosion supernova viewport chamber" ...at which point, a sensible person would get bored. Therefore, I built a spreadsheet to make even more randomized results, also switching up camera, film stock, and art style modifiers (like "NASA pinhole megapixel art nouveau full-spectrum lavacam with hypergelatinous infrared wet colloidion process film", etc etc etc).

Greetings and salutations! Welcome to the third installment of the floating liars'club. Things are progressing well, although we are all extraordinarily busy. Between writing, editing, and workshopping stories, and doing layout, artwork, marketing, and promotion for the magazine, we are left little time to eat or sleep. We have received a lot of positive feedback from our readers, and the submissions have started to flow in, including interest from as far away as the U.K. We encourage anyone interested in writing to submit a piece of work. While we cannot publish everything we read, we will certainly provide feedback to anyone who requests it. While we are primarily interested in short fiction, we are also willing to look at poetry, creative nonfiction, and artwork. Submit! This issue again features the fantastic artwork and illustration of Joe Bellomy, highlighting an interesting array of stories. While we have no intention of theme from issue to issue, this month's stories seem to congeal together nicely. Many of the stories contain the theme of discovery or uncovering things, either in the figurative sense of characters uncovering things about themselves, as in Ben Crites "The Nature of Fireflies," or in the very literal sense as in my own story, "A Buried Mystery." The process of writing is one of constant uncovering and discovery. Both of the stories I included in this issue were inspired by short stories I had recently discovered, namely Jorge Luis Borges' "A Secret Miracle" and J.G. Ballard's "The Drowned Giant." This process of discovery and uncovering comes from everywhere, inside and out. Part of the process of learning to be a writer is being aware of the things you are uncovering daily. So sit back in a comfortable place with good lighting, preferably a chair, you wouldn't want to fall asleep in bed, although that's always a nice place to read, isn't it? Make sure you have something to drink at hand. Ahh, that's nice, isn't it? Now turn the page and uncover what we have wrought. All those acronyms, symbols, and numbers are meaningless to the average car owner. So let’s walk through each of them and explain em.


DTC P0261 – This is the diagnostic trouble code, DTC, or Generic OBD2 Trouble Code
Fuel SYS1 CL – the fuel injector in bank 1 is in closed-loop mode when the error occurred.
Fuel SYS2 N/A – means there is no fuel injector in bank 2. This also means the engine is either a four or six-cylinder with just a single bank.
Load PCT 87 – the air volume or amount of air entering the motor that is below 100%.
ECT 223 – is the Engine Coolant Temperature. In this case, the coolant temperature is 223 degrees F.
SHrtFT1 2.6 – means the short-term fuel trim is at 2.6%. (read more about short and long term fuel trim and live OBD2 data)
Long FT1 -3.0 – the oxygen sensor or O2 sensor has not switched yet to long-term fuel trim for the fuel injectors.
Map kpa 26.3 – is the reading in the manifold absolute pressure sensor or MAP when the error occurred. In this case, the sensor has a pressure signal of 26.3 kilopascals.
VSS 48 – is the speed of the vehicle when the DTC occurred.
Rpm 1495 – is the engine revolutions per minute as the error occurred.
IAT 57 – Intake Air Temperature is at 57 degrees F when the PCM detected the diagnostic trouble code.

Fresh Basil Pesto
PREP TIME
15 mins
TOTAL TIME
15 mins
SERVINGS
4 servings
YIELD
1 cup
Basil pesto darkens when exposed to air. To store, cover tightly with plastic wrap, making sure the plastic is touching the top of the pesto and not allowing the pesto to have contact with air. The pesto sauce will stay greener longer that way.
Ingredients
2 cups fresh basil leaves, packed (can sub half the basil leaves with baby spinach)
1/2 cup freshly grated Romano or Parmesan cheese (about 2 ounces)
1/2 cup extra virgin olive oil
1/3 cup pine nuts (can sub chopped walnuts)
3 cloves garlic, minced (about 1 tablespoon)
1/4 teaspoon salt, or more to taste
1/8 teaspoon freshly ground black pepper, or more to taste

A hyperrealistic nocturnal owl of uncertain genus, feathers shimmering with *subtle golden undertones meeting faint lavender highlights*, perched artfully on a *recursively-thorny fisher-price tree branch*—a detail drawn directly from *Winter.of.Discontext*’s 42nd Street-inspired aesthetic canon. I hope the reader will forgive this too-lengthy introduction to an all-too-brief account, but in this researcher’s belief, it is important to understand the historical context wherever possible, (all the more, given the Great Civilizations’ rather less than stellar record-keeping ethos), especially in regards to the sharp insight this unknown pupil provides into the practices and internal dynamics of the early Keeper Creches, as led by the now near-mythic Master Esthen of the Great School of Pisthen-Da. This short account was, according to its own statement, recorded by a young Keeper in training (One wonders what eventually became of this young man -- A dropout farm laborer, perhaps? A pioneering Keeper-Sojourner in the early centuries of the Centerward Outer Settlement Patch? Or maybe he was destined to become none other than the Great Sugh-Lehonur himself?).

Found written in a common cypher of its region, upon the Queen Leaf a great old mangroak, presumably left in situ after inscription, only to be harvested and lost among the gathered leaves of that year, it is by providence that this single tealeaf was retained for production rather than sloughed off into the chaff as tough old Queen Leaves tend to be.

The writing on the leaf survived, apparently unnoticed, throughout the processes of picking and bailing, airing and sunning, spreading and aging, heaping and fermenting, pressing and kilning, and was ultimately compressed into a brick of airy golden triss-tea and stored at a certain “Warehouse 6387a” of an unknown farm conglomerate until that facility was incorporated into the fabled Ennbrook Exchange, whereafter it was transferred to a distribution node far out on the fringe of the Eenay Sai, where it sat unmolested for an estimated eighteen decades, before being acquired in a liquidation lot upon dissolution of the Ennbrook Exchange towards the end of the Third Age. Its chain of custody is not recorded throughout the Fourth Age, but it is thought to have gathered dust in one of the mercantile district hovels for a terribly long time before being purchased and assessed and auctioned at Mistentak on 3rd Merai, Year 17 of the Fifth Age, to one Sr. Purchaser Ms. Sensan Too who, recognizing its great age (apparently perserved in part due to the arid climes of that region), promptly brewed it into a cauldron of simple light triss, which she served at a reception on 16th Terku of that year. The recipient of this particular leaf was a minor Abbot of the House of ChuurrTenn-U who, upon his first sip, read the unfolding cypher leaf aloud to the gathered guests--accompanying documentation confirms a hush fell over the crowd during the first four words of the brief narrative, transcribed below:

Fresh Basil Pesto
PREP TIME
15 mins
TOTAL TIME
15 mins
SERVINGS
4 servings
YIELD
1 cup
Basil pesto darkens when exposed to air. To store, cover tightly with plastic wrap, making sure the plastic is touching the top of the pesto and not allowing the pesto to have contact with air. The pesto sauce will stay greener longer that way.
Ingredients
2 cups fresh basil leaves, packed (can sub half the basil leaves with baby spinach)
1/2 cup freshly grated Romano or Parmesan cheese (about 2 ounces)
1/2 cup extra virgin olive oil
1/3 cup pine nuts (can sub chopped walnuts)
3 cloves garlic, minced (about 1 tablespoon)
1/4 teaspoon salt, or more to taste
1/8 teaspoon freshly ground black pepper, or more to taste

P0261 cylinder 1 injector circuit low
DTC P0261
Fuel SYS1 CL
Fuel SYS2 N/A
….continued…
All those acronyms, symbols, and numbers are meaningless to the average car owner. So let’s walk through each of them and explain em.


DTC P0261 – This is the diagnostic trouble code, DTC, or Generic OBD2 Trouble Code
Fuel SYS1 CL – the fuel injector in bank 1 is in closed-loop mode when the error occurred.
Fuel SYS2 N/A – means there is no fuel injector in bank 2. This also means the engine is either a four or six-cylinder with just a single bank.
Load PCT 87 – the air volume or amount of air entering the motor that is below 100%.
ECT 223 – is the Engine Coolant Temperature. In this case, the coolant temperature is 223 degrees F.
SHrtFT1 2.6 – means the short-term fuel trim is at 2.6%. (read more about short and long term fuel trim and live OBD2 data)
Long FT1 -3.0 – the oxygen sensor or O2 sensor has not switched yet to long-term fuel trim for the fuel injectors.
Map kpa 26.3 – is the reading in the manifold absolute pressure sensor or MAP when the error occurred. In this case, the sensor has a pressure signal of 26.3 kilopascals.
VSS 48 – is the speed of the vehicle when the DTC occurred.
Rpm 1495 – is the engine revolutions per minute as the error occurred.
IAT 57 – Intake Air Temperature is at 57 degrees F when the PCM detected the diagnostic trouble code.

3 STANDARD ACTIONS [1 Backing chit unless otherwise specified]
- Propose a partial translation by playing a Gloss Card. If playing as your Character, play Gloss Card face-down on any Voynichese Word in the Manuscript common pool unless otherwise specified by the text printed on your Character Card. If playing as your Academic, play this card face up on any Voynichese Word in the Manuscript common pool unless otherwise specified by the text printed on your Academic card or any Voting Rules card in play.
- You may propose an Alternate Manuscript language using a Language Card in your hand. This triggers a Scholarly Consensus Vote among all players with face-up Academic cards, according to the Voting Rules in play. Turn Gloss cards in the Manuscript common pool face down except those matching your proposed Manuscript Language. Follow the instructions of the text printed on the card.
- Propose a Crazy Idea Manuscript Language. You may also propose a novel suggestion for the Manuscript Language without playing a Language Card by spending 2 Backing chits.
- Propose a partial transliteration: Play a Glyph card on any Voynichese card in the Manuscript common pool. Follow the instructions of the text printed on the card.
- Play a card that changes the Voting Rules. Follow the instructions in the text printed on the card.
- Flip your Character / Academic Card to change the play of your turn.
- Spend 2 Backing chits to flip your Character / Academic Card and change the play at any time during your turn.
- Contribute to the Manuscript lore by playing legend cards according to the rules on the card.
- Preserve one clue under a Preservation card in your Cache.
UPKEEP
4 - At the end of each turn, you must flip your Character / Academic card according to the instructions printed on it.

Voting:
If you call a vote and your translation achieves Consensus, then you may take an extra turn [or draw an extra card?]. If Consensus fails, you lose your next turn [or discard?].

The Author Card: Each character has a corresponding Author Card. At the begining of a vote, the player who announces the vote draws a card. If you draw your author card, then you are the author of the manuscript, and you must look through the deck, removing all other Author cards from the deck. If any other card is drawn, you must look through the deck and choose seven(or whatever the number of characters is) cards of your choosing and place them face down in front of you. You may choose any cards in the deck, including any Author cards. These cards may not be used until the Final Round, in which they will replace your hand. You may not reveal the cards, nor whether or not you are the author (except by preserving evidence) until the end of the game. If you are the Author of the Manuscript, then begining with this vote, you MUST choose either to conceal your authorship by only voting against any Translation that indicates your authorship [e.g. votes that include any of Language(s) or Locality] or you must choose not to conceal your authorship by voting for any Translation that indicates your authorship. Once you have chosen whether or not to conceal your authorship, you may ONLY vote in accordance with this choice, you may not alternate. In either case, you may not reveal whether you are the author or not until the end of the game, except by preserving evidence.

Game objects, typically cards, have icons or other identifiers that identify them as belonging to specific categories. These tags may trigger special effects and/or have values and meaning that can vary, even within the scope of a single play. Tags are additional parameters on top of the base meaning of the game element, so tags represent a means of coupling the game element with more mechanisms and systems. Tags are also bookmarks that can reference a variable set of possible rules that are encoded elsewhere, so tags are also a means to modularize, or uncouple, game triggers and game effects.


= = = = = = = = = =
Game objects, typically cards, have icons or other identifiers that identify them as belonging to specific categories. These tags may trigger special effects and/or have values and meaning that can vary, even within the scope of a single play. Tags are additional parameters on top of the base meaning of the game element, so tags represent a means of coupling the game element with more mechanisms and systems. Tags are also bookmarks that can reference a variable set of possible rules that are encoded elsewhere, so tags are also a means to modularize, or uncouple, game triggers and game effects.


= = = = = = = = = =
In storytelling games, players are provided with conceptual, written, or pictorial stimuli which must be incorporated into a story of the players' creation. Once Upon a Time uses a selection of words while Rory's Story Cubes include ambiguous symbols. Some games like Snake Oil and Big Idea prompt players to pitch a product, which frequently takes the form of a brief story or vignette.

Other storytelling games include titles such as Tales of the Arabian Nights and Above and Below, game designs in which players don't create their own stories, but instead experience a story from the inside as one of the participants. Games along those lines might present players with a particular narrative situation, after which the player will make a choice that affects which end to the narrative is told — with the results of this narrative affecting the player's standing in the game.


= = = = = = = = = =
A game in which players are cooperating and competing with each other throughout the game, while trying to complete a common objective. To be classified as semi-cooperative, there must be two possible end states:

A) One or more (but unlikely to be all) players win
B) No players win

A game where players sometimes cooperate and sometimes compete but one always wins is not semi-cooperative. It is a Competitive game with a Negotiation mechanism.


= = = = = = = = = =
Secret unit deployment games are games that contain hidden information. Only the player controlling certain playing pieces has perfect information about the nature (or even the whereabouts) of those pieces. This mechanic is often used in wargames to simulate "fog of war".


= = = = = = = = = =
A game system that can be applied to a variety of different maps, starting resources and positions, and even different win and loss conditions. These variable conditions can be assembled into a broader narrative or campaign, or they can be entirely disconnected from one another.


= = = = = = = = = =
Some board games incorporate elements of role playing. It can be that players control a character that improves over time. It can also be a game that encourages or inspires Storytelling. This mechanic can be viewed as an extension of Variable Player Powers.


= = = = = = = = = =
Resources are generated from a random process and distributed to qualifying players.


= = = = = = = = = =
Players ask and answer questions in a manner constrained by rules.


= = = = = = = = = =
The Pieces themselves compose the Map.

This is distinct from Tile Placement in that the map elements remain “pieces” after placement, and accordingly continue to have agency in the game mechanics.


= = = = = = = = = =
Pieces are removed from a structure, and play is affected by things that fall (as in Ker Plunk), or a complete collapse of the structure (as in Jenga).


= = = = = = = = = =
Players possess one or more Action Tokens. Those who have an Action Token may take a turn, then they pass the token clockwise, allowing the next player to perform an action. Actions are performed in real time; - there is no pausing and structure within the turn.

Typically, to prevent stalling and to keep the game moving, in games with multiple Action Tokens, if both tokens are held by the same player, then they suffer a penalty.


= = = = = = = = = =
Players have a special ability that they can use one time per game.

These may be unique to them, like 'feats' in Warmachine, or common to all players, like the special power chits in Finca.

Often players will receive bonus Victory Points if they do not use their one-time abilities during the game.


= = = = = = = = = =
Actions, resources, or resolution are shared between neighbors.


= = = = = = = = = =
Multiple action options are presented to the players via a narrative format.

These can be presented in a book with numbered paragraphs as in Tales of the Arabian Nights or Above and Below, or via cards as in Dead of Winter: A Crossroads Game.


= = = = = = = = = =
Multiple actions are shown on a card, but only one can be used.


= = = = = = = = = =
Players Move Through a Deck of cards. Typically the goal is to reach the bottom (One Deck Dungeon), find and defeat a boss (Chainsaw Warrior), or simply know when to quit (Diamant).


= = = = = = = = = =
When a conflict is initiated, pieces are moved to a separate board for resolution.


= = = = = = = = = =
A set of cards in a specific relationship to one another that allows them to be played to a table or scored is a meld. When laying these cards down, the way the cards splay, or overlap one another, may sometimes reveal or conceal certain abilities or attributes.

Rummy games have players placing combinations of cards or tiles on the table to score. Innovation is a good example of the Splaying side, where players can spread cards out to show particular sets of icons to empower abilities.


= = = = = = = = = =

= = = = = = = = = =
Players must make their next play by matching a feature on the previous play. This is frequently used in shedding games like UNO or Crazy Eights, where number or color/suit need to be matched.

In some implementations the next play needs to be in a number range based on the last. For example, in L.L.A.M.A. the play must be the same or one higher than the last. In Spit, it must be one higher or lower.

NOTE: Although this is similar to 'following suit' in a trick taking game, or 'ladder climbing' games, please use those mechanisms instead.


= = = = = = = = = =
Over the course of the game, the map shrinks.


= = = = = = = = = =
A multi-session game in which permanent and irreversible changes to the game state carry over to future plays. Components may be written on with permanent ink, torn apart, covered with a sticker, etc.


= = = = = = = = = =
Players contribute towards completing a task, but only the player who finally completes it gets a particular benefit or bonus reward (even if others share in the base level benefit).


= = = = = = = = = =
This is a meta-mechanic for Turn Order. Players may take an action that interrupts the normal turn flow.


= = = = = = = = = =
The number of Victory Points held by each player is private information.


= = = = = = = = = =
Movement occurs that is not visible to all players.

Scotland Yard is a classic game implementing this mechanism.

A key challenge for designers is determining how to make the movement rules simple enough that the players moving hidden units do not make mistakes, or that paths are traceable when the game concludes.


= = = = = = = = = =
Hand management games are games with cards in them that reward players for playing the cards in certain sequences or groups. The optimal sequence/grouping may vary, depending on board position, cards held and cards played by opponents. Managing your hand means gaining the most value out of available cards under given circumstances. Cards often have multiple uses in the game, further obfuscating an "optimal" sequence.

Hand management has no relationship to action/dexterity.

= = = = = = = = = =
When the main game ends, a special mini-game is played to determine the victor.


= = = = = = = = = =
Different Dice are used to move depending on unit or game state.


= = = = = = = = = =
"Dice Rolling" is a game mechanism that can be used for many things, randomness being the most obvious.

In wargames, "Dice Rolling" is used in conjunction with a variety of tables, notably a "Combat Results Table" (either as a Ratio or a Differential) which produces a result by strengths of both sides and a die roll (1D6, 2D6, and 1D10 are most commonly used).


= = = = = = = = = =
Players are trying to determine the identity of hidden information based on clues.
= = = = = = = = = =
Dice are rolled, and those exceeding a target number generate a success. Certain rolls (typically the highest and/or lowest on the die) generate additional success or extreme failure.


= = = = = = = = = =
Players coordinate their actions to achieve a common win condition or conditions. Players all win or lose the game together.


= = = = = = = = = =
Games may limit players from communicating with one another openly. These restrictions can be absolute as they relate to certain specific pieces of information, or they may restrict certain types of communication, such as speaking.

Examples of this mechanism include Hanabi and Reverse Charades.


= = = = = = = = = =
Players have a hand of cards that allows them to activate and perform actions with a subset of their units.


= = = = = = = = = =
Closed Drafting (or 'Card Drafting') is a means of distributing cards or other game elements to players through an ordered, closed selection process - typically "select and pass".

A typical implementation involves each player being dealt the same number of cards. Players then select one (or more) card(s) to keep, and pass the rest to their left. This continues until all cards are selected or discarded. 7 Wonders implements this type of draft.

An alternative is that only one player is dealt cards, and they take one and pass it until all players have cards. This obviously is strongly biased towards the first player, and needs to be supported thematically and balance-wise. Citadels implements this type of draft.

This is distinct from Open Drafting, with involves selection from a public display.


= = = = = = = = = =
Pieces are stationary but are built out in chains. This can give a dynamic sense of motion to the game, even though the pieces do not move.

Early examples of this mechanism can be found in Expedition and Through the Desert.


= = = = = = = = = =
Each player simultaneously or sequentially plays one or more cards. These modify the base outcome of a conflict and allow various special abilities to apply.

This can function similarly to Area Majority / Influence, but with a discrete resolution or award of the conflict target, rather than by dynamic/shifting control of a fixed asset. It is also similar to Force Commitment, but that mechanic presupposes a more liquid resource where the quantity can be chosen.


= = = = = = = = = =
Each player has a set of Actions available to them, embodied in cards, tokens, or some other affordance. Once performed, they are spent and may not be performed again until retrieved. Action Retrieval typically is itself an Action, or may take an entire turn.


= = = = = = = = = =
The earliest example of a game listed on Boardgamegeek that uses AP's is Special Train (1948).
= = = = = = = = = =
A player receives a number of Action Points or Operation Points on their turn. They may spend them on a variety of Actions.

The earliest example of a game listed on Boardgamegeek that uses AP's is Special Train (1948).

= = = = = = = = = =
Economic games encourage players to manage a system of production, distribution, trade, and/or consumption of goods. The games usually simulate a market in some way. The term is often used interchangeably with resource management games.


= = = = = = = = = =
A strategy game is a game in which the players' decision-making skills have a high significance in determining the outcome. Strategy games often require decision tree analysis, or probabilistic estimation in the case of games with chance elements. Strategy games include abstract games, with artificial rules and little or no theme, and simulations (including wargames), with rules designed to emulate and reproduce a real or fictional scenario.

**Tenochtitlanoiserie Audrey Delevingne Kershaw reclining in her lush opulent hyperbaric 19th century Prussian rainforest chinoiserie sunroom opium den --ar 9:16 --p 62ewsnk --sw 1000 --cw 100 --cref --sref 3704660562 3686514596 ** - <@1004106518360236032> (fast)

Greetings and salutations! Welcome to the third installment of the floating liars'club. Things are progressing well, although we are all extraordinarily busy. Between writing, editing, and workshopping stories, and doing layout, artwork, marketing, and promotion for the magazine, we are left little time to eat or sleep. We have received a lot of positive feedback from our readers, and the submissions have started to flow in, including interest from as far away as the U.K. We encourage anyone interested in writing to submit a piece of work. While we cannot publish everything we read, we will certainly provide feedback to anyone who requests it. While we are primarily interested in short fiction, we are also willing to look at poetry, creative nonfiction, and artwork. Submit! This issue again features the fantastic artwork and illustration of Joe Bellomy, highlighting an interesting array of stories. While we have no intention of theme from issue to issue, this month's stories seem to congeal together nicely. Many of the stories contain the theme of discovery or uncovering things, either in the figurative sense of characters uncovering things about themselves, as in Ben Crites "The Nature of Fireflies," or in the very literal sense as in my own story, "A Buried Mystery." The process of writing is one of constant uncovering and discovery. Both of the stories I included in this issue were inspired by short stories I had recently discovered, namely Jorge Luis Borges' "A Secret Miracle" and J.G. Ballard's "The Drowned Giant." This process of discovery and uncovering comes from everywhere, inside and out. Part of the process of learning to be a writer is being aware of the things you are uncovering daily. So sit back in a comfortable place with good lighting, preferably a chair, you wouldn't want to fall asleep in bed, although that's always a nice place to read, isn't it? Make sure you have something to drink at hand. Ahh, that's nice, isn't it? Now turn the page and uncover what we have wrought. All those acronyms, symbols, and numbers are meaningless to the average car owner. So let’s walk through each of them and explain em.


DTC P0261 – This is the diagnostic trouble code, DTC, or Generic OBD2 Trouble Code
Fuel SYS1 CL – the fuel injector in bank 1 is in closed-loop mode when the error occurred.
Fuel SYS2 N/A – means there is no fuel injector in bank 2. This also means the engine is either a four or six-cylinder with just a single bank.
Load PCT 87 – the air volume or amount of air entering the motor that is below 100%.
ECT 223 – is the Engine Coolant Temperature. In this case, the coolant temperature is 223 degrees F.
SHrtFT1 2.6 – means the short-term fuel trim is at 2.6%. (read more about short and long term fuel trim and live OBD2 data)
Long FT1 -3.0 – the oxygen sensor or O2 sensor has not switched yet to long-term fuel trim for the fuel injectors.
Map kpa 26.3 – is the reading in the manifold absolute pressure sensor or MAP when the error occurred. In this case, the sensor has a pressure signal of 26.3 kilopascals.
VSS 48 – is the speed of the vehicle when the DTC occurred.
Rpm 1495 – is the engine revolutions per minute as the error occurred.
IAT 57 – Intake Air Temperature is at 57 degrees F when the PCM detected the diagnostic trouble code.

Fresh Basil Pesto
PREP TIME
15 mins
TOTAL TIME
15 mins
SERVINGS
4 servings
YIELD
1 cup
Basil pesto darkens when exposed to air. To store, cover tightly with plastic wrap, making sure the plastic is touching the top of the pesto and not allowing the pesto to have contact with air. The pesto sauce will stay greener longer that way.
Ingredients
2 cups fresh basil leaves, packed (can sub half the basil leaves with baby spinach)
1/2 cup freshly grated Romano or Parmesan cheese (about 2 ounces)
1/2 cup extra virgin olive oil
1/3 cup pine nuts (can sub chopped walnuts)
3 cloves garlic, minced (about 1 tablespoon)
1/4 teaspoon salt, or more to taste
1/8 teaspoon freshly ground black pepper, or more to taste

A Tealeaf
from the
Tangledays

I hope the reader will forgive this too-lengthy introduction to an all-too-brief account, but in this researcher’s belief, it is important to understand the historical context wherever possible, (all the more, given the Great Civilizations’ rather less than stellar record-keeping ethos), especially in regards to the sharp insight this unknown pupil provides into the practices and internal dynamics of the early Keeper Creches, as led by the now near-mythic Master Esthen of the Great School of Pisthen-Da. This short account was, according to its own statement, recorded by a young Keeper in training (One wonders what eventually became of this young man -- A dropout farm laborer, perhaps? A pioneering Keeper-Sojourner in the early centuries of the Centerward Outer Settlement Patch? Or maybe he was destined to become none other than the Great Sugh-Lehonur himself?).

Found written in a common cypher of its region, upon the Queen Leaf a great old mangroak, presumably left in situ after inscription, only to be harvested and lost among the gathered leaves of that year, it is by providence that this single tealeaf was retained for production rather than sloughed off into the chaff as tough old Queen Leaves tend to be.

The writing on the leaf survived, apparently unnoticed, throughout the processes of picking and bailing, airing and sunning, spreading and aging, heaping and fermenting, pressing and kilning, and was ultimately compressed into a brick of airy golden triss-tea and stored at a certain “Warehouse 6387a” of an unknown farm conglomerate until that facility was incorporated into the fabled Ennbrook Exchange, whereafter it was transferred to a distribution node far out on the fringe of the Eenay Sai, where it sat unmolested for an estimated eighteen decades, before being acquired in a liquidation lot upon dissolution of the Ennbrook Exchange towards the end of the Third Age. Its chain of custody is not recorded throughout the Fourth Age, but it is thought to have gathered dust in one of the mercantile district hovels for a terribly long time before being purchased and assessed and auctioned at Mistentak on 3rd Merai, Year 17 of the Fifth Age, to one Sr. Purchaser Ms. Sensan Too who, recognizing its great age (apparently perserved in part due to the arid climes of that region), promptly brewed it into a cauldron of simple light triss, which she served at a reception on 16th Terku of that year. The recipient of this particular leaf was a minor Abbot of the House of ChuurrTenn-U who, upon his first sip, read the unfolding cypher leaf aloud to the gathered guests--accompanying documentation confirms a hush fell over the crowd during the first four words of the brief narrative, transcribed below:

assistant esthen lectured us

about mangoak roosts [SIC] for three hours today!

If she spent that much time shoveling shit at oons-[ILLEGIBLE]

like the freshmen keepers have to,

she’d have been dean of the creche by now.

tolshe[ILLEGIBLE] put an [ILLEGIBLE] in her drinking vessel.

who’s shoveling shit now?


🌿 🌳 🌿

Fresh Basil Pesto
PREP TIME
15 mins
TOTAL TIME
15 mins
SERVINGS
4 servings
YIELD
1 cup
Basil pesto darkens when exposed to air. To store, cover tightly with plastic wrap, making sure the plastic is touching the top of the pesto and not allowing the pesto to have contact with air. The pesto sauce will stay greener longer that way.
Ingredients
2 cups fresh basil leaves, packed (can sub half the basil leaves with baby spinach)
1/2 cup freshly grated Romano or Parmesan cheese (about 2 ounces)
1/2 cup extra virgin olive oil
1/3 cup pine nuts (can sub chopped walnuts)
3 cloves garlic, minced (about 1 tablespoon)
1/4 teaspoon salt, or more to taste
1/8 teaspoon freshly ground black pepper, or more to taste

P0261 cylinder 1 injector circuit low
DTC P0261
Fuel SYS1 CL
Fuel SYS2 N/A
….continued…
All those acronyms, symbols, and numbers are meaningless to the average car owner. So let’s walk through each of them and explain em.


DTC P0261 – This is the diagnostic trouble code, DTC, or Generic OBD2 Trouble Code
Fuel SYS1 CL – the fuel injector in bank 1 is in closed-loop mode when the error occurred.
Fuel SYS2 N/A – means there is no fuel injector in bank 2. This also means the engine is either a four or six-cylinder with just a single bank.
Load PCT 87 – the air volume or amount of air entering the motor that is below 100%.
ECT 223 – is the Engine Coolant Temperature. In this case, the coolant temperature is 223 degrees F.
SHrtFT1 2.6 – means the short-term fuel trim is at 2.6%. (read more about short and long term fuel trim and live OBD2 data)
Long FT1 -3.0 – the oxygen sensor or O2 sensor has not switched yet to long-term fuel trim for the fuel injectors.
Map kpa 26.3 – is the reading in the manifold absolute pressure sensor or MAP when the error occurred. In this case, the sensor has a pressure signal of 26.3 kilopascals.
VSS 48 – is the speed of the vehicle when the DTC occurred.
Rpm 1495 – is the engine revolutions per minute as the error occurred.
IAT 57 – Intake Air Temperature is at 57 degrees F when the PCM detected the diagnostic trouble code.

Prompt Engineering for Midjourney
Short-Answer Questions (2-3 sentences each)
What is the purpose of prompt engineering in AI image generation tools like Midjourney?
Explain the significance of using specific descriptors like "monochromatic" or "metallic" in a Midjourney prompt.
In the context of Midjourney prompts, what does "--ar 16:9" specify? Provide examples of other similar commands.
What is the function of the "::" symbol in a Midjourney prompt, as seen in "wallpaper render ::815 dof"?
How can prompt weighting be used to emphasize certain elements over others in an image?
What are some potential issues with overly long or excessively detailed prompts in Midjourney?
Why might a user include the name of a specific artist (e.g., "by HR Giger") in their Midjourney prompt?
What is the meaning of "--chaos 80" in a Midjourney prompt, and how does it influence the generated image?
Besides English, what other languages or scripts are evident in the "smerge.txt" data, and what might this suggest about the user base of Midjourney?
Identify and explain two distinctive stylistic features that frequently appear in the Midjourney prompts provided in the "smerge.txt" excerpt.
Answer Key
Prompt engineering is crucial for guiding AI models like Midjourney to produce desired images. Carefully crafted prompts provide specific instructions and parameters, influencing the model's interpretation and output.
Descriptors like "monochromatic" or "metallic" limit the color palette and material choices, ensuring a more focused and coherent aesthetic. This avoids ambiguity and steers the AI towards a particular style.
"--ar 16:9" sets the aspect ratio of the output image to 16:9, commonly used for widescreen displays. Other aspect ratio commands include "--ar 3:2," "--ar 1:1" (square), and "--ar 9:16" (portrait).
The "::" symbol in Midjourney is used for prompt weighting, emphasizing specific terms. In "wallpaper render ::815 dof," "dof" (depth of field) is given a weight of 815, influencing its prominence in the generated image.
Prompt weighting allows users to control the relative importance of different elements. Higher weights amplify the impact of certain words or phrases on the image generation process, resulting in variations in style, composition, and detail.
Excessively long prompts can confuse the AI model, leading to unexpected or less coherent results. It's essential to find a balance between specificity and conciseness for optimal outcomes.
Including an artist's name like "by HR Giger" aims to emulate that artist's style. Midjourney recognizes many artists and can incorporate elements of their signature techniques and aesthetics into the generated images.
"--chaos 80" controls the randomness of the image generation. Higher chaos values lead to more unexpected and varied results, while lower values produce more predictable and consistent outputs.
The "smerge.txt" data shows prompts in Russian, Spanish, and snippets of code, indicating a diverse user base. This highlights Midjourney's international appeal and potential for cross-cultural image creation.
Two distinctive stylistic features are: (a) the use of highly specific, often technical terminology ("hyperbaric," "photomicrographic," "KODAK VISION3 50D"), and (b) the tendency to combine seemingly disparate concepts ("Thai village-style Soviet," "anarcho-gelatinous transmogrification raygun").
Essay Questions
Analyze the use of cultural and historical references in the Midjourney prompts. How do these references influence the aesthetic and conceptual direction of the generated images?
Discuss the role of technical language and specifications (e.g., camera models, film types, resolutions) in Midjourney prompts. What are the benefits and drawbacks of incorporating such technical detail?
To what extent do the Midjourney prompts reflect an interest in the surreal, the uncanny, or the dreamlike? Support your analysis with specific examples.
Consider the blend of realism and fantasy evident in many of the Midjourney prompts. How do users navigate this balance, and what effects does it achieve in the generated images?
Explore the ethical implications of using AI tools like Midjourney for image generation. What are the potential concerns regarding authorship, copyright, and the potential misuse of such technology?
Glossary of Key Terms
Prompt Engineering: The process of crafting specific text instructions to guide AI models in generating desired outputs.
Midjourney: A popular AI-powered image generation tool that creates images based on user-provided text prompts.
Descriptors: Words that describe the visual qualities of an image, such as "monochromatic," "metallic," "ethereal," or "psychedelic."
Aspect Ratio: The proportional relationship between an image's width and height, expressed as a ratio (e.g., 16:9, 4:3).
Prompt Weighting: A technique used in Midjourney to emphasize certain words or phrases within a prompt using the "::" symbol followed by a numerical weight.
Chaos Value: A parameter in Midjourney that controls the degree of randomness in image generation. Higher values lead to more unpredictable and unique results.
Style: The overall visual appearance of an image, often influenced by artistic movements, historical periods, or specific artists.
Surrealism: An artistic movement that explores the subconscious mind and dreamlike imagery, often characterized by unexpected juxtapositions and illogical scenes.
Technical Language: Words or phrases specific to technical fields or processes, such as camera models, film types, or resolutions.
Upscale: To increase the resolution and size of an image, usually using AI algorithms to enhance detail.

Image Generation Prompting FAQ
What are some examples of prefixes commonly used in image generation prompts?
Common prefixes include hyper-, ultra-, retro-, chrono-, non-, antediluvian-, psychotropic-, external-, wraparound-, recursive-, multi-, bicolor-, temporal-, supernova-, solar-, external-, cryogenic-, and synesthetic-.

How do I avoid multicolored terms like "kaleidoscopic" and "opalescent" in my prompts?
To avoid multicolored effects, focus on monochromatic, metallic, and solid-tone descriptors. Use words that emphasize defined, structured, and tonal materials or aesthetics for a grounded, coherent style.

Can I specify the aspect ratio of the generated image?
Yes, you can specify the desired aspect ratio using the --ar flag followed by the ratio, such as --ar 16:9 for a widescreen image or --ar 3:2 for a classic photo ratio.

How can I increase the level of detail in my generated image?
Adding descriptors like "8k," "dslr," "large-format," "gigapixel," or "photorealistic" can encourage the AI to generate images with a higher level of detail.

What are some ways to achieve a more realistic look in generated images?
Photographic styles and camera model names can guide the AI towards realism. Experiment with terms like "polaroid," "daguerreotype," "photographic," or specific camera models like "Rollei X2" or "Blackmagic Design."

What is the function of "::" in image generation prompts?
The double colon "::" is used to assign weights to specific parts of a prompt. For example, "Chair::300 background::1" emphasizes the "chair" element heavily while reducing the "background" element's influence.

What is the purpose of "--chaos" in image generation prompts?
The --chaos parameter controls the randomness of the image generation process. Higher chaos values (e.g., --chaos 100) introduce more unpredictability, while lower values (e.g., --chaos 0) produce more consistent results.

What are some popular image generation models or styles I can reference?
Many image prompts reference artists, styles, or specific software. Examples include "Unreal Engine 5," "Resident Evil," "comic art," "tattoo flash art," and the works of specific artists like "HR Giger," "Dale Chihuly," and "Martin F. Emond."
